summary.text: A derecho is a widespread, long-lived, straight-line wind storm tied to a fast-moving complex of severe thunderstorms, and it brings hurricane-force winds, heavy rain and flash floods.
Unlike an ordinary gust front, its winds stay up for longer, often strengthen after they start, and the storm system can stay active for many hours or even days.
On radar, classic derechos show bow- or spearhead-shaped squall lines, which bulge outward because descending air builds a small high-pressure area behind the line.

facts.label: Name means
facts.value: "Straight" in Spanish, versus a tornado's twisted wind

facts.label: NWS wind threshold
facts.value: At least 25 m/s (50 kn) for six hours or more

facts.label: Damage swath (newer definition)
facts.value: At least 100 km wide and 650 km long

items.prompt: Someone says a derecho is just a normal gust front with a fancy name. What actually sets a derecho apart?

Its winds always fade within the first minutes

items.explain: Derecho winds remain sustained for longer than conventional gust fronts, often increase in strength after onset, and may reach hurricane force.

items.prompt: A camper says, "Derechos are daytime storms, so we're safe once the sun goes down." How right is that?

Partly, they are rare but possible at night

items.explain: Derechos are equally likely during day and night.

items.prompt: On radar, a long line of storms starts bulging forward into a backward "C". What is pushing the middle out?

options.label: Warm air rising ahead of the storms
A tornado spinning inside the line
The ground heating up under the line
Sinking air building high pressure behind it

items.explain: Squall lines bow out because strong descending air behind the line forms a small high-pressure system in the rain area.

items.prompt: A storm chaser spots a derecho made of several bows strung along one big squall line. Compared with a single-bow derecho, what extra danger is more likely?

options.label: Large hail the size of houses
Tornadoes from embedded supercells
A drop to freezing temperatures
A storm surge along the coast

items.explain: Multi-bow serial derechos contain embedded supercells, so tornadoes can spin out of them.

items.prompt: Why did meteorologists bring in a stricter, more physical definition of "derecho"?

options.label: Too few storms were ever studied by radar
The word was being used for loosely organized wind events
Derechos had stopped happening in the United States
The Spanish name was considered too confusing

paragraphs.heading: A straight-line windstorm
paragraphs.text: A derecho is a broad, long-lasting windstorm whose winds blow in a straight line rather than spinning. It comes from a fast-moving cluster of severe thunderstorms that meteorologists call a mesoscale convective system. The name is the Spanish word for 'straight', in contrast to the twisted wind of a tornado. A derecho can bring winds as strong as a hurricane's, along with heavy rain and flash floods.

paragraphs.heading: Staying power
paragraphs.text: A derecho races along in the direction its parent storms are heading, the way a gust front does. The difference is staying power. A derecho's winds last longer, and they often grow stronger after they first arrive, sometimes reaching the force of a tornado or a hurricane. The storm system behind one can keep going for many hours, and now and then for several days.

paragraphs.heading: When they strike
paragraphs.text: Derechos are mainly a warm-weather event. In the Northern Hemisphere most arrive in June, July and August; in the Southern Hemisphere the busy months are March, April and May. They favour places where the air is fairly unstable and the vertical wind shear is fairly strong. Still, a derecho can happen in any month, and one is just as likely by night as by day.

paragraphs.heading: The bow on the radar
paragraphs.text: On weather radar, a classic derecho shows up as a squall line, a band of storms in a line or gentle curve, that bends into a bow or a spearhead. These shapes are called bow echoes or spearhead echoes, and a bow looks like a backward letter C. The line bulges forward because strong sinking air behind it builds a small zone of high pressure in the rainy area at its back. That sinking air can arrive as a downburst. The strongest winds usually blow just behind the front edge of the line, where the wind shifts and the pressure jumps.

paragraphs.heading: Naming and defining it
paragraphs.text: The word entered science in 1888, when Gustavus Detlef Hinrichs used it in the American Meteorological Journal. His paper was based on a major derecho that crossed Iowa on 31 July 1877. Over time the label was sometimes stuck on wind events that were neither well organised nor long-lived, so meteorologists worked out a tighter definition. The US National Weather Service calls it a derecho when a band of storms keeps winds at or above 25 m/s (50 kn) across its whole front for at least six hours. A newer definition also asks for bow echoes on radar and a path of damage no less than 650 km (400 miles) long and 100 km (60 miles) wide.

paragraphs.heading: Serial, progressive and hybrid
paragraphs.text: Derechos come in a few kinds. A serial derecho usually goes with a very deep low, and it holds either one huge bow echo or several bows set inside a long squall line; the several-bow kind is much more common. A progressive derecho is a bow-shaped line of storms that may travel hundreds of miles along a stationary front, like the August 2020 Midwest derecho. Tornadoes can spin out of serial derechos because of supercells buried inside them, but they form less often in the progressive kind. A hybrid derecho mixes features of both.
